request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]     MRN: [REDACTED]     DOB: [REDACTED]     Admission Date: [REDACTED]     Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with complaints of chest pain, shortness of breath, and a productive cough. Upon examination, the patient was found to have tachycardia and tachypnea. Laboratory findings revealed leukocytosis with elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. CT chest showed left lower lobe pneumonia and a large pericardial effusion. The patient received appropriate treatment for pneumonia and underwent transthoracic echocardiogram to further characterize the effusion as moderate circumferential pericardial effusion.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
Upon consultation with the patient’s psychiatrist, clozapine was stopped, which was thought to be the cause for the non-resolving pericardial effusion. Following the discontinuation of the drug, there was a gradual improvement in the respiratory status. The patient was discontinued from clozapine and discharged to home in stable and improved condition.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care provider for future management of high cholesterol and assistance with smoking cessation.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
None prescribed at this time.

FOLLOW-UP STUDIES:
Transthoracic echocardiogram to be repeated for further evaluation in one year.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
Stable and improved.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: I31**

The record supports either of two codes, so this is a judgement call:

- **Pericardial effusion (I31).** After the pneumonia was treated, the effusion did not resolve. The team attributed it to clozapine and stopped the drug. Breathing then gradually improved and the patient was discharged. The pericardial effusion therefore appears to be the condition chiefly responsible for the episode. Under ICD-10-AM rules for an adverse effect of a drug taken as prescribed, you code the condition itself. Clozapine is then recorded as an additional external cause code, not as the principal diagnosis.
- **Pneumonia (J18).** This is the main alternative. CT showed left lower lobe pneumonia and it was treated.

Two cautions:

- The discharge diagnosis section is withheld, so I cannot confirm which condition the clinicians documented as principal.
- The raised CRP and ESR could point to clozapine-induced pericarditis rather than a simple effusion. If so, the code would be I30 (acute pericarditis). Without the documented diagnosis, I31 fits the record best.
